questions.q: What is the correct syntax for a CSS rule that makes all `<h2>` elements have red text color and a font size of 24 pixels?
questions.a:
Correct answer: `h2 { color: red; font-size: 24px; }`  
A wrong answer like `h2 { color=red; font-size=24px; }` (using `=` instead of `:`) or `h2 { color: red; font-size: 24px }` (missing semicolon after last declaration) reveals the student confuses CSS declaration syntax with HTML attribute syntax or doesn't know that each declaration must end with a semicolon (though the last one is optional, it's best practice). Another common error: `h2 { color: red; font-size: 24px; }` written as `h2 { color: red; font-size: 24px }` without braces — shows misunderstanding of the rule set structure (selector + declaration block).

questions.q: Explain the difference between a class selector (`.highlight`) and an ID selector (`#main-heading`) in terms of (a) how many elements they can target in a valid HTML document, and (b) specificity weight in the cascade.
questions.a:
Correct answer: (a) A class selector can target **multiple** elements (any element with `class="highlight"`), while an ID selector must target **at most one** element (since `id` values must be unique per page). (b) ID selector has **higher specificity** (1,0,0) than class selector (0,1,0), so if both apply conflicting styles to the same element, the ID selector's declarations win regardless of order.  
A wrong answer that says "both can target multiple elements" shows the student doesn't know the uniqueness constraint of `id`. Saying "class has higher specificity" reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of the cascade — a critical error for board exams where specificity questions appear frequently.

Correct answer: **green** Reasoning: 1. All four rules target the same `

Highest specificity wins: `#intro` (1,0,0) > `.note` and `.important` (0,1,0) > `p` (0,0,1). 4. Therefore `color: green` from `#intro` applies. A wrong answer of "red" (thinking last rule wins) shows the student believes cascade order overrides specificity — a classic trap. "Blue" or "black" indicates they don't know how to calculate specificity or that ID beats class.

questions.q: Compare the descendant combinator (` `) and child combinator (`>`) in CSS selectors. Write a selector that targets only `<li>` elements that are **direct children** of a `<ul>` with class `menu`, but not `<li>` elements nested deeper inside sub-menus.
questions.a:
Correct answer: `.menu > li`  
Explanation: The child combinator `>` selects only **direct children**. The descendant combinator (space) selects **any descendant** at any depth. So `.menu li` would select all `<li>` inside `.menu` including those in nested `<ul>`, while `.menu > li` selects only the top-level list items.  
A wrong answer like `.menu li` (missing `>`) shows the student doesn't distinguish between direct child and any descendant — a common error when styling navigation menus. Another error: `.menu > ul > li` would select the wrong level.

Correct answer: **No, it is not good practice.** Removing `outline` on `:focus` (`outline: N/A;`) makes the button invisible to keyboard-only users (who navigate via Tab key), violating WCAG 2.1 Success Criterion 2.4.7 (Focus Visible). The `:hover` style helps mouse users, but keyboard users get no visual indication of focus.  
Better: `button:focus { outline: 2px solid #0056b3; outline-offset: 2px; }` — keeps visible focus ring but styles it.  
A student who says "it's fine because hover works" or "outline looks ugly so remove it" shows they prioritize aesthetics over accessibility — a major misconception. Board exams increasingly test accessible design principles.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you have built a webpage for your school's cultural fest using HTML (nodes 001-005) — it has headings, paragraphs, a ______ form, a table of events, and images.
What is CSS (Cascading Style Sheets)? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is a stylesheet language used to describe the presentation of an HTML document.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about CSS (Cascading Style Sheets)?
questions.a: Misconception: "CSS properties like margin, padding, and border work the same way on all HTML elements, including inline elements like <span> and <a>." Why it's wrong: Inline elements ignore vertical margins/padding (top/bottom) and height/width properties.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to write a complete CSS rule set (selector + declaration block) that styles a given HTML structure using at least three different selector types (element, class, ID, attribute, pseudo-class) and five distinct properties, and explain how the cascade resolves conflicting declarations for the same element.
